notes: \cpara{Opens with the Catholic Church as, ``Perhaps,'' the largest voluntary institution: one held together by its members' gifts, not by taxes or salaries.}

\cpara{Lists what holds the Church together: the fear of hell, ``affective death spirals'' around ideas and leaders, and conformity at weekly meetings. Most of these are named in passing, with links to the author's earlier posts.}

\cfact{Broadly the scholarly view. The Hebrew Bible's Sheol is described as a place where both the righteous and the unrighteous dead go, ``regardless of their moral choices in life'' (Wikipedia, ``Sheol'').}

\clogic{Stated without a hedge and without evidence. The linked post, ``No, Really, I've Deceived Myself'' (2009), describes one conversation with a woman who was ``Nominally \ldots\ an Orthodox Jew,'' not a theologian.}
\cpara{Points back to ``Why Our Kind Can't Cooperate'': self-described rationalists think themselves above such bonds. An observation of the community, offered as such.}
\cpara{The practical contrast: for a simple relief effort, such as help after a tidal wave in Thailand, the Pope could mobilize far more people than Richard Dawkins.}
\cpara{Draws the consequence, as a conditional: while this holds, gains for atheism at Catholicism's expense are partly hollow.}
\cpara{Grants the Church's harms: opposition to condoms, money spent on religion, and the cost of prayer. The link for the last is to a Reuters story of 25 March 2009 that I could not open.}

\cfact{This was news that month. On 17 March 2009, on the flight to Cameroon, Pope Benedict XVI said AIDS could not be overcome ``through the distribution of condoms, which even aggravates the problems'' (\textsc{The Guardian}, 17 March 2009).}
\cpara{Grants that avoiding harm is a victory, and says in the next line that it is an empty one if it is the only one.}
\cpara{The post's central question, asked as a question: setting harm aside, does the average Catholic do more good than the average atheist, simply by being more active?}

\cfact{For information, American survey data then available pointed to yes for religious practice in general. In a survey of 2000, people who attended services weekly gave on average \$2,210 a year, against \$642 for those who attended rarely or had no religion. They were also more likely to give to nonreligious causes (71 against 61 percent) and to volunteer for them (60 against 39 percent) (Arthur Brooks, \textsc{Policy Review}, 2003). Brooks's groups are defined by attendance, not by denomination or belief.}
\cpara{Grants that choosing efficient causes could make up for less effort, and observes, hedged (``few of us''), that few actually do it.}
\cpara{States an objection in the reader's voice: people who fear eternal hell may simply be more motivated than any rationalist can be.}

\cpara{Concedes the objection's possibility with care: a rational agent can copy a winning policy only if it can choose its own motivation, so ``some false beliefs'' may motivate more than any true one. The concession is stated conditionally (``it may be'', ``it is possible'').}
\cpara{Admits, as a joke against itself, that going on with the question is a ``motivated continuation.''}
\cpara{Argues that fear of hell is an imperfect motivator: believers still sin, and reproach themselves as smokers do.}

\cfact{The ego-depletion account linked here later failed two large preregistered replications; the note on ``Superstimuli and the Collapse of Western Civilization'' gives the details. The observation that believers sin despite fearing hell does not depend on it.}

\cpara{Argues by question (``who says'') that caring about real goals could move people as much as heaven does, since no one can picture an infinite reward anyway. The paragraph argues that a match is possible, not that it happens.}
\cpara{Proposes that techniques from CBT and meditation, combined with a cause worth caring about, might let rationalists keep up.}

\cfact{Stated without a hedge, and the two cases differ. For CBT it was well supported: a 2006 review of 16 meta-analyses found large effects for depression and several anxiety disorders (Butler and colleagues). For meditation the evidence was weaker. A 2007 review for the US Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality found ``813 predominantly poor-quality studies''; meta-analyses of low-quality studies showed that Zen meditation lowered blood pressure, but ``Firm conclusions on the effects of meditation practices in healthcare cannot be drawn.''}
\cpara{Labels the proposal a speculation, ``not a technique I can use right now,'' and states its purpose: an illustration of not giving up on rationality at the first disadvantage.}
\cpara{The post's main hypothesis, hedged (``I suspect''): the Church's output comes less from fear of damnation than from people meeting in person.}

\cfact{Later survey evidence fits this suspicion. Robert Putnam and David Campbell's \textsc{American Grace} (2010) found religious Americans more generous, including to secular causes. In a PBS interview Putnam summarized the reason: ``If you have a lot of friends at church, you are very likely to be a more generous person''; according to PBS's summary, belief that God would punish them ``wasn't a factor.''}
\cpara{Applies the hypothesis to a scattered community. The five-mile claim is offered as a bet (``I bet''), not a finding.}
\cpara{Announces the next day's post (``Church vs. Taskforce'', 28 March 2009), and wonders whether video calls could substitute for meeting, while suspecting they could not.}
\cpara{Admits that fighting akrasia alone may not work: ``I'm not sure that's even true.''}
\cpara{Restates the proposal, hedged (``I suspect''): regular in-person meetings, for motivation rather than coordination.}

\cfact{For information, among American denominations Catholics are a low benchmark for giving. A 2008 review of the research found that it ``consistently shows that theologically conservative Protestants tend to give the most money while Catholics tend to give the least'' (Lincoln, Morrissey and Mundey, University of Notre Dame).}
\cpara{Proposes two norms: applaud caring strongly about something, and expect people to do something useful with their lives.}

\cpara{Estimates, hedged (``I don't think it's remotely unrealistic''), that half the Catholic effort, better aimed, could do twice the good. The next paragraph gives a related guess: that most of the Church's money goes to religion.}

\cpara{Guesses (``I would venture'') that the Church spends more than half its earnings on religious activity, and derives a norm of giving 5\% of income to ``real'' causes: the non-religious half of a 10\% tithe. No figures are given for the guess.}

\cfact{For information, the suggested tithe is not what most American churchgoers give. In the 1998 General Social Survey, ``only 9.4 percent of religious GSS respondents tithed, and 71.7 percent donated less than two percent of their income'' (as reported in the 2008 Notre Dame review). A 5\% norm would exceed what most of those respondents gave in total.}
\cpara{Ends on the nearer goal: secular humanists should first at least match the believers' good works per head.}
